checks.claim: On the Origin of Species first published 1859
checks.note: First published 24 November 1859 by John Murray.

checks.claim: 'Survival of the fittest' is Herbert Spencer's phrase
checks.note: Spencer coined it in Principles of Biology (1864).

checks.claim: 'Ten years later he took up' the phrase (i.e. 1869)
checks.note: True of the Origin only: the phrase enters its fifth edition in 1869 ('Natural Selection, or the Survival of the Fittest'). But Darwin agreed to Wallace's suggestion to adopt it in July 1866, and first used it in print in The Variation of Animals and Plants under Domestication (1868): 'Mr. Herbert Spencer has well expressed the same idea by the Survival of the Fittest.' So he took it up nine years on, not ten. Fix: 'and ten years later, in the book's fifth edition, he took up Herbert Spencer's phrase for it' (or 'nine years later').

checks.claim: Key: the fittest stag is the one that fathers the most fawns (fitness = reproductive success)
checks.note: Fitness is the capacity to contribute genes to the next generation; 'survival alone, without reproduction, yields zero fitness contribution.'

checks.claim: Wrong choices (wins most fights, runs fastest, lives longest) are not what biologists mean by fittest
checks.note: Berkeley lists the misconception that the fittest are the strongest, fastest or largest; the stem separates fighting, speed and longevity from fathering fawns, so only the key measures fitness.

checks.claim: Context: traits that suit the surroundings leave more young and grow more common over generations
checks.note: Berkeley: fitness is 'its ability to get its genes into the next generation'; individuals better able to survive leave more descendants.

checks.claim: Darwin kept every breed he could buy and joined two London pigeon clubs
checks.note: Origin ch. 1: 'I have kept every breed which I could purchase or obtain' and 'permitted to join two of the London Pigeon Clubs.'

checks.claim: Fantail has thirty or even forty tail feathers vs twelve or fourteen
checks.note: Darwin's words, matched closely.

checks.claim: Breeds look as different as wild species do
checks.note: Darwin: at least twenty breeds would be ranked as well-defined species by an ornithologist who did not know their origin.

checks.claim: Key: Darwin concluded all breeds came from one wild species, the rock pigeon
checks.note: 'I can feel no doubt that all our domestic breeds have descended from the Columba livia' (with its geographical sub-species); Grokipedia agrees: 'all traceable to the wild rock-pigeon' (https://grokipedia.com/page/On_the_Origin_of_Species).

checks.claim: Wrong choices (a species per breed; two or several wild species crossed) were views Darwin rejected
checks.note: Darwin argued against descent from several aboriginal stocks and against crossing as the source: crossing gives only forms intermediate between the parents.

checks.claim: Context quote 'man's power of accumulative selection'
checks.note: Darwin's own words in ch. 1.

checks.claim: Context: most fanciers he met thought each main breed came from its own wild species
checks.note: Darwin said he never met a fancier 'who was not fully convinced that each main breed was descended from a distinct species'; 'most' understates it but is true.

checks.claim: Context: the Origin opens with such breeds
checks.note: Chapter 1, Variation under Domestication, with the pigeons at its heart.

checks.claim: About nine in ten of Gorongosa's elephants killed during the war years
checks.note: 2,542 elephants in 1972, 242 by 2000 (about 90%); Princeton: 'from over 2,500 to around 200 after the war'; Africa Geographic: 'around 90% of the region's elephants.'

checks.claim: Killed by ivory hunters
checks.note: Combatants poached elephants 'for ivory and meat', ivory selling for arms. 'Ivory hunters' is a fair simplification; the selective pressure on tusks was the ivory.

checks.claim: Before the war nearly one female in five tuskless; by 2000 about half
checks.note: Campbell-Staton et al., Science 2021: 18.5% (n = 52) to 50.9% (n = 108), a nearly threefold rise over the 28 years 1972-2000 (Africa Geographic: 'over 28 years'). Berkeley: 18.5% was 'the situation in 1972' and 'over half the female elephants in Gorongosa were tuskless in the year 2000.' 18.5% = nearly one in five; 50.9% = about half. The flagged figure checks out.

checks.claim: Key: tuskless females were spared and passed the trait on
checks.note: Tuskless females 'more than five times as likely to survive to reproduce'; the trait is inherited (an X-linked gene version, lethal in males).

checks.claim: Wrong choices (females stopped growing tusks, tusks shrank in a lifetime, fear stunted the young's tusks) are all wrong
checks.note: Lamarckian or individual-change explanations; the paper shows selection on an inherited trait.

checks.claim: Context: populations evolve, not individuals
Wild cabbage (Brassica oleracea) is in the mustard family and can be weedy
checks.note: Family Brassicaceae; Grokipedia says it can persist as a weed in disturbed ground.

checks.claim: Wild cabbage grows on seaside cliffs in western Europe, and farmers bred that plant into the vegetables
checks.note: The plant does grow on Atlantic sea cliffs (Grokipedia, Wikipedia). But the largest genetic study (Mabry et al., Molecular Biology and Evolution 2021, 224 accessions) found the Aegean B. cretica the closest wild relative, 'supporting an origin of cultivation in the Eastern Mediterranean', and judged the 'wild' western European B. oleracea populations to be feral, i.e. escaped descendants of the crops, not their ancestors. Grokipedia's own page flags this conflict. The stem's chain 'grows on cliffs in western Europe ... farmers bred it' implies those cliff plants are the ancestor, which the newest work disputes. Fix: drop the place, e.g. 'Wild cabbage, a plant of the mustard family, is the wild form of one species that farmers bred into several vegetables...', or say 'a wild cabbage of the Mediterranean'.

checks.claim: Key: broccoli came from selecting the biggest clusters of flower buds
checks.note: Italica group (broccoli): edible flower heads; cauliflower (Botrytis): condensed inflorescence.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: cabbage (terminal bud), kohlrabi (swollen stem), Brussels sprouts (axillary buds) were not selected for flower-bud clusters
checks.note: Brussels sprouts are leafy side buds, not flower buds, so they are not defensible; cauliflower, the other flower-cluster crop, is not offered.

checks.claim: Context: kale from leaves, cabbage from the tip bud, kohlrabi from the stalk, Brussels sprouts from side buds; all one species
checks.note: Matches the cultivar groups; all are B. oleracea and interbreed freely.

checks.claim: Context: 'Many textbooks call the wild plant wild mustard'
checks.note: True as a report (the Exploratorium says the crops come 'from a wild mustard plant'). It is a loose name: 'wild mustard' properly names other plants, chiefly charlock (Sinapis arvensis; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sinapis_arvensis). Suggest: 'Many textbooks loosely call the wild plant wild mustard, though that name belongs to other plants; all these vegetables...'.

checks.claim: Chihuahua under 3 kg, Great Dane over 70 kg
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'from Chihuahuas under 3 kg to Great Danes over 70 kg'.

checks.claim: Robert Wayne's team compared dog DNA with wolves, coyotes and jackals in the 1990s
checks.note: Vila, Wayne et al., Science 1997: mtDNA of 162 wolves and 140 dogs of 67 breeds, with coyotes and golden and black-backed jackals sampled; STLPR: every coyote and jackal sequence differed from every dog sequence 'by at least 20 sites' (https://www.stlpr.org/health-science-environment/2017-11-19/on-science-evolution-of-the-family-dog).

checks.claim: Key: wolves alone, small and large breeds alike
checks.note: Wayne: 'Dogs are domesticated wolves'; the 67 breeds spanned all sizes. Grokipedia: all modern dogs trace to an extinct wolf population close to the grey wolf.

checks.claim: Wrong choices (jackals for small breeds; a wolf-coyote-jackal mix; coyotes for some breeds) are wrong
checks.note: No coyote or jackal ancestry in dogs is recognised; these are the old Darwin and Lorenz views the context names.

checks.claim: Context: dogs tamed at least 15,000 years ago from an ancient wolf population
checks.note: Grokipedia: 15,000-40,000 years ago; Wikipedia: about 15,000-30,000 years ago. 'At least 15,000' is safe.

checks.claim: Context: Darwin thought wolves, coyotes and jackals might all have played a part
checks.note: In Variation under Domestication (1868) Darwin named C. lupus and C. latrans (the coyote) plus several jackals as probable ancestors.

checks.claim: Context: Konrad Lorenz thought some breeds came from jackals
checks.note: Man Meets Dog (1949; English 1954): some dogs descended from wolves, some from jackals.

checks.claim: Teosinte is a wild grass of Mexico
checks.note: Grasses native to Mesoamerica; maize's ancestor, Balsas teosinte, is Mexican.

checks.claim: Teosinte ears hold about a dozen kernels or fewer, each in a stony case
checks.note: UW-Madison: 'just 10 to 12 kernels'; Wikipedia: five to 10 segments, each with one seed in 'a very hard fruitcase'.

checks.claim: A change in one gene (tga1) leaves the kernel bare
checks.note: 'A single nucleotide change in the teosinte glume architectural gene (tga1)' removed the casing, 'exposing the edible golden kernel'; Grokipedia Maize agrees (naked grains).

checks.claim: Key: farmers planted seed from the plants with the change
checks.note: People chose 'by growing more of the plants they preferred.'

checks.claim: Wrong choices: cracking cases (acquired, not inherited), roasting changing the gene, crossing with wheat
checks.note: None is defensible; wheat was domesticated in the Fertile Crescent about 10,000 years ago (https://grokipedia.com/page/Wheat) and reached the Americas only with Columbus's second voyage (1493), thousands of years after maize began.

checks.claim: Context: began in southwestern Mexico about 9,000 years ago
checks.note: Balsas River Valley, about 9,000 years ago (Grokipedia also gives 9,000-10,000).

checks.claim: Key: the bacteria became resistant, as resistant ones lived and multiplied
checks.note: Berkeley: resistance arises when variation gives some bacteria a better chance to survive the drug and they leave more descendants; 'bacteria do not evolve resistance to our antibiotics because they "try" so hard.'

checks.claim: Wrong choices: her body or her immune system became resistant; each bacterium learned to stand the drug
checks.note: WHO: 'bacteria - not humans or animals - become resistant'; no bacterium learns or adapts in its lifetime by effort (Berkeley).

checks.claim: Context: a 2015 WHO survey found three people in four thought the body becomes resistant
checks.note: November 2015, about 10,000 people (9,772) in 12 countries: 'Three quarters (76%) of respondents think that antibiotic resistance happens when the body becomes resistant to antibiotics.'

checks.claim: A new insect spray (DDT) came into wide use in the 1940s and at first worked well against houseflies
checks.note: Insect-killing power found by Paul Muller in 1939; US military use from 1943, wide farm use after 1945.

checks.claim: By 1947 flies in parts of Europe were surviving it and the spraying was failing
checks.note: 'By 1947 housefly resistance to DDT had evolved'; Grokipedia puts Italian houseflies resistant by 1946 (https://grokipedia.com/page/Pesticide_resistance); reports from Sweden (Wiesmann, 1947) and Italy (Sacca and Missiroli, 1947, who blamed resistant flies for 'the failure of DDT to control flies in Italy').

checks.claim: Key: flies raise many generations in a single year
checks.note: Egg to adult 'in as few as 7-10 days under optimal warm conditions', 'enabling 10-12 or more generations annually in favorable climates'; Grokipedia's pesticide page: 'short generation times enable rapid adaptation.'

checks.claim: Wrong choices: each fly grew tougher; the spray changed the flies' genes; the poison wears off on small flies
checks.note: Resistance comes from selection of 'rare individuals possessing pre-existing genetic variations', not from flies toughening or the poison directing genes; the size answer does not explain spreading resistance.

checks.claim: Context: about ten days egg to adult, ten or more generations a year
checks.note: 7-10 days; 10-12 or more generations in warm climates.

checks.claim: Context: more than 500 kinds of insect have evolved resistance to some pesticide
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'over 500 insect species' (also 500+ arthropod species, 632 in the resistance database); Wikipedia: over 500 species of pests. Figure grows over time but 'more than 500' stays true.

checks.claim: Kettlewell marked moths with paint under the wings
checks.note: 'marked them underneath their wings with cellulose paint'.

checks.claim: A soot-blackened wood near Birmingham, then a clean lichen-covered wood in Dorset
checks.note: Cadbury Bird Reserve near Rubery, Birmingham, 'heavily polluted' (1953); Deanend Wood, Dorset, 'well covered with lichens' (1955).

checks.claim: Key: the moths matching the bark came back more often (wrong choices: same form wins in both woods, or no difference)
checks.note: Birmingham: dark 27.5% vs pale 13% recaptured; Dorset: pale 13.7% vs dark 4.7% (Wikipedia) or 12.5% vs 6.3% (Grokipedia). The result reversed between woods, so all three wrong choices are wrong.

checks.claim: Context: about twice as many, or more, of the matching moths recaptured
checks.note: Ratios 2.1 (Birmingham) and 2.0-2.9 (Dorset) by share recaptured; in Birmingham also by raw count (about 123 of 447 dark vs 18 of 137 pale).

checks.claim: Context: Niko Tinbergen filmed birds taking the moths
checks.note: Tinbergen filmed the work and 'captured live footage of birds eating moths'.

checks.claim: Context: the dark form was rare before soot, and by 1895 about 98 in 100 around Manchester
checks.note: First melanic caught near Manchester in 1848; about 98% of moths in the Manchester area by 1895 (Wikipedia agrees).

checks.claim: Critics: Kettlewell's moths were set on tree trunks at densities far above the wild
checks.note: Trunks argued to be abnormal resting sites; releases far denser than natural populations (Grokipedia: wild density about 40-50 per square km).

checks.claim: Majerus re-tested it for six years in his garden near Cambridge
checks.note: Cook et al. 2012: 'Majerus released 4864 moths in his six-year experiment'; a 1 ha rural garden at Springfield, near Coton, Cambridgeshire. Wikipedia frames it as 2001-2007 (release data run 2002-2007).

checks.claim: Each night a dozen moths settled on branches; at dawn he watched for birds
checks.note: 'Each night one moth was released into each of the 12 netting sleeves surrounding a branch'; sleeves removed before dawn; moths gone 4 h after sunrise counted as eaten, with birds seen eating them through binoculars. Wild moths rest mostly on branches (over half, Wikipedia).

checks.claim: Key: birds ate more dark moths than pale (wrong choices: more pale, equal, bats ate nearly all)
checks.note: 'Strong differential bird predation against melanic peppered moths'; bats (pipistrelles, 419 moths) took both forms without significant difference, so the bat choice is wrong.

checks.claim: Context: nine kinds of bird, robins and blue tits among them
checks.note: Robins, hedge sparrows, great tits, blue tits, blackbirds, starlings, wrens, magpies and a lesser spotted woodpecker.

checks.claim: Context: dark form near Cambridge fell from about 12 in 100 to 1 over those years
checks.note: Madingley trap samples: 0.12 in 2001 to 0.01 in 2007 (0.10 in 2002, the first release year); 'about 12' fits the 2001-2007 framing.

checks.claim: Context: Majerus died in 2009; four colleagues published in 2012 as the most direct evidence yet
checks.note: L. M. Cook, B. S. Grant, I. J. Saccheri and J. Mallet, Biology Letters 2012: 'the most direct evidence yet to implicate camouflage and bird predation'. Not in quotation marks in the context, and paraphrased fairly.

checks.claim: Context: a 2002 book's charge of cheating was examined and found without merit
checks.note: Judith Hooper, Of Moths and Men (2002); 'Scientists have examined the allegations made by Hooper, and found them to be without merit.'

unit_notes: No errors; two uncertain, each with a one-line fix. (1) b6a4b37f38: Darwin first printed 'survival of the fittest' in 1868 (Variation under Domestication), nine years after the Origin; 'ten years later' is true only of the Origin's fifth edition (1869), so name the edition. (2) 6d1ae00de0: the largest genetic study (Mabry et al. 2021) puts the crops' origin in the eastern Mediterranean (closest wild relative B. cretica) and finds western European 'wild' cliff cabbage feral; drop 'grows on seaside cliffs in western Europe' as the ancestor's home. The 'wild mustard' line is true as a report of textbooks, but it would be clearer to say it is a loose name (wild mustard properly names charlock). Flagged checks confirmed: Gorongosa 18.5% to 50.9% tuskless females over 1972-2000 (Campbell-Staton et al. 2021), so 'nearly one in five' and 'about half by 2000' stand; Kettlewell's 'about twice, or more' stands in both woods; Majerus's experiment is 'six-year' in the 2012 paper (Cook, Grant, Saccheri, Mallet), 4,864 moths, 12 sleeves a night, nine bird species, carbonaria 12% (2001) to 1% (2007). PMC and the Science paper blocked direct fetches; the paper's text was read through the Europe PMC REST full text and the Princeton, Berkeley and Africa Geographic summaries.
